catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Phonetics and Phonology', sec. 2.1 Tones (2.1.1-2.1.4), pp. 12-15; chapter TOC 2.1 Tones / 2.2 Vowels / 2.3 Consonants / 2.4 Contrastive Sounds / 2.5 Ad…
catalog_quote: 2.1.1 There are four lexically distinctive tones in Mao Naga. It is a register system with all the four tones being pretty level. We name the distinctive pitch ievels High tone. Lower High tone. Mid tone [or Higher Low] and Low tone ... 2.1.2 The system is fairly nonrestricted. Tone has unconstrained occurrence with all vowels and word positions. While there are no constraints of tonotactics in disyllables-al! the sixteen combinations are attested in abundance - the sixty four tonotactic configurations possible in trisyllables in a four tone system are not attested basically because the occurrence of trisyllables is much less numerous ... 2.1.3 All the four tones can occur in singlelexical units. ... 2.1.4 Tones may free-vary

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (four level register tones on every syllable, no word-stress rule stated, domain not stated by the source) rests on the only reference grammar of the language (Giridhar 1994, CIIL, 502 pp), which we hold as scanned text; the deciding quotation (2.1.1-2.1.4) and the intonation footnote are present verbatim at the stated sections/pages. Glottolog lists no other grammar or phonology for maon1238; open database and repository searches found no tone/stress/instrumental study of Mao Naga proper; a 2008 NEHU linguistics dissertation by a Mao speaker (downloaded) independently calls Giridhar the only comprehensive description and confirms the language is tonal; the 2014 vowel paper (downloaded) is silent on prosody. Nothing suggests a stress or accent system that would change the classification. No action needed.
